messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi's eyes would often glaze over as he recounted the memories of his childhood. Growing up in a household where domestic violence was a frequent occurrence had left an indelible mark on him. He remembered the sound of shattering glass, the feeling of being frozen in place, and the image of his mother cowering in the corner. These snapshots would replay in his mind like a broken record, each moment etched in vivid detail. As he grew older, Kofi tried to make sense of what had happened. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he was somehow responsible for not being able to protect his mother. This lingering sense of helplessness now manifested as an overwhelming fear of not being able to stop bad things from happening to those around him. When memories of the past flooded back, Kofi's body would react as if he were still in the same position, frozen and powerless. The memories also made him acutely aware of potential dangers lurking in every corner. Unusual silence would send his mind racing, making him feel like something was off. He'd notice people acting suspiciously or spot potential weapons in seemingly innocuous objects – a pencil could become a shiv, a broken bottle a lethal projectile. These perceived threats would heighten his sense of alertness, but also made him question his own sanity. Feeling uncomfortable in unfamiliar places became a familiar pattern for Kofi. As a police officer, he was expected to be confident and composed in the face of uncertainty. But when confronted with new environments or unexpected situations, Kofi's mind would spiral back to those memories of childhood helplessness. He couldn't rely on himself, he thought; what if he froze up again? What if he failed to protect someone? When people touched him unexpectedly, Kofi's body would react as if it was reliving the past all over again. The tactile sensation sent his mind racing back to those memories of feeling powerless and trapped. It was as if his body had a memory of its own, one that refused to let go. Kofi tried to navigate these emotions on his own, but they only seemed to intensify with time. His fear of losing control and going crazy drove him further into avoidance behaviors – sticking to familiar routines, avoiding social gatherings, and hesitating to take on new assignments at work. Yet, this self-imposed exile only reinforced the notion that he couldn't trust himself. It was when Kofi's commanding officer confronted him about his recent performance decline that the weight of these memories finally became too much to bear. The shame and fear he felt brought him to seek help – not just for his own sake but also for those around him whom he might put in harm's way due to his inability to cope. As Kofi sat in the therapist's office, recounting his story, it was clear that these experiences had woven a tangled web of emotions and memories. He knew he needed to untangle this knot, but what scared him most was facing the possibility that those memories would forever define him – and that he might never be able to shake off the feeling of being trapped in that childhood nightmare.
